list.listitem: Functional dyspepsia (FD) is a multifactorial constellation of symptoms and is not a disease entity itself. The etiology of the symptoms is poorly understood. C

Patients over age 60 years with new onset dyspepsia and patients at increased risk for malignancy (e.g., high-incidence region or family history) should be referred for prompt esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD). B

Patients under the age of 60 years should be tested for Helicobacter pylori (HP) and treated, if positive. Treatment may eradicate the infection but, in those with FD and no underlying undetected ulcer, it is unlikely to resolve the symptoms. B

For those who are HP negative or who have persistent symptoms following HP eradication, initiate empiric therapy with a proton pump inhibitor (PPI), tricyclic antidepressant (TCA), prokinetic agent (in that order) or psychotherapy; if not successful, consider endoscopy. B

background.definition: Non-ulcer dyspepsia is a functional gastrointestinal (GI) disorder characterized by upper Gl symptoms in patients without endoscopic or sonographic evidence of structural disease (e.g., peptic ulcer disease, gastroesophageal reflux, gallbladder disease). Functional GI disorders are considered to be a product of interactions between psychosocial factors and altered gut physiology via gut-brain interactions. These disorders are classified by GI symptoms related to motility disturbance, visceral hypersensitivity, altered mucosal and immune function, altered gut microbiota, altered central nervous system processing, or any combination of these. Dyspepsia is pain or discomfort that is centrally localized in the upper abdomen. Symptoms may include epigastric burning, early satiety, upper abdominal bloating, nausea, and postprandial fullness.

list.listitem: New-onset dyspepsia occurs in 2.8% of adults per year.
Women have a higher incidence of dyspepsia than men (14/1000 vs.10/1000 per yea), Hispanics have a higher risk, and the incidence of dyspepsia increases with age.
FD affects up to 16% of healthy individuals in the general population.
Authors of a systematic review of 24 studies identified a similar prevalence estimate of 16.3% (95% CI, 9.1%-25.1%.
Among ambulatory patients undergoing EGD for uninvestigated dyspepsia in São Paulo, Brazil, FD was found in 66% (20% with normal endoscopy results and 46% with gastritis).

Prevalence of at least one functional GI disorder among school children in Columbia was 21.2%. Prevalence was significantly lower using ROME IV criteria compared to Rome III, although prevalence of FD increased.
Overall, global prevalence of uninvestigated dyspepsia is 21%, which varies among countries and according to the criteria used to define it.
Among 65,569 patients in the Disease Analyzer database with an initial diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome, 6% had an overlap with FD.

The causes of FD are not well understood and are likely multifactorial. Symptoms have been attributed to changes in secretion, motility, and sensation or perception of gastric function (acid hypersensitivity) in the context of stress and biological influences.
Observational studies report associations between dyspepsia and HP infection, NSAID/ASA use, unemployment, cigarette smoking, and social stressors.
Apart from NSAIDs and antibiotics, there is little evidence to support medications as an etiology for dyspepsia.

Dietary factors should be considered. In one RCT with 412 participants, mean age 48 years, of whom 36.7% reported bloating at baseline, those randomized to high sodium intake of 150 mmol/d had an increased risk of bloating (RR 1.27; 95% CI, 1.06-1.52). In addition, those randomized to the high-fiber 32 g/day DASH diet also had an increased risk of bloating over the 3 sodium levels (RR 1.41; 95% CI, 1.22-1.64); the effect was more pronounced in men.
Almost half (45%) of patients with hetertopic pancreas (ectopic pancreatic tissue) who presented with abdominal pain had dyspepsia.
The proposed pathophysiology includes altered level of serum pepsinogen, visceral hypersensitivity, immune system dysregulatoin and alteration in gut microbiome.
A higher level of serum pepsinogen, the inactive precursor of the proteolytic enzyme pepsin, is associated with both HP infection and dyspeptic symptoms.

Visceral hypersensitivity is one proposed mechanism. In one study, the median capsaicin dose required to cause moderate pain was significantly lower in patients with FD vs. healthy controls. Authors of another study using 5 cohorts of patients with either irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) or FD, found a consistent increase in GI symptom severity associated with increasing GI sensitivity, independent of anxiety/depression comorbidity.

Immune system activation/dysregulation is seen in both functional gastrointestinal disorders and atopy; atopic conditions are seen in excess among patients with FD over control patients (OR 1.41; 95% CI, 1.26-1.58). Mucosal inflammatory infiltrate is dominated by mast cells, eosinophils and intraepithelial lymphocytes in the intestines of patients with functional GI disorders. Authors of a systematic review of 51 papers found evidence supporting increases in proportions of gut-homing T lymphocytes in both FD and IBS indicating that a loss of mucosal homeostasis may drive the symptoms.

In one study of 2000 patients with functional GI disorders, there was an association between GI symptoms and production of gas such as hydrogen and methane, suggesting an alterations in the microbiome or mechanical and chemical sensitization.
Although the quality of evidence is low, one meta-analysis of 7 studies with 263 patients suggested a link between FD and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.

The disorder of duodenal microecology such as greater microflora diversity, different microflora structure, different microflora composition, specific taxa and specific microbiome function may be the mechanism for FD.

Diagnosis is based on clinical symptoms of upper abdominal discomfort or pain associated with bloating, nausea, early satiety, or belching without evidence of structural disease; however, physical examination is not reliable for identifying a specific cause of dyspepsia. C
Refer patients for EGD if they are over age 60 years with new onset dyspepsia or at increased risk for malignancy due to residency in a high-risk country for gastric cancer or family history. B

Patients under age 60 years should undergo noninvasive HP stool antigen or urea breath testing. If positive, eradication is recommended, although resolution of symptoms is highly variable and probably depends on the presence or absence of undetected underlying ulcer. B

Gastric cancer risk assessment using endoscopic and histological methods provide comparable results. Therefore, having a normal or mild grade of atrophy on EGD avoids the need for histological mapping.

Differential.Differential_Features: Associated changes in stool frequency and characteristics
Dull aching pain that awakes the patient at night
Vomiting rather than abdominal pain and epigastric fullness

list.listitem: Rome IV criteria, published in May 2016, were again determined through a Delphi method using experts in the field. The purpose was to create a positive definition of functional GI disorders. The 33 adult and 20 pediatric disorders are classified primarily based on symptoms rather than physiologic criteria. Functional dyspepsia (FD) is classified under Gastroduodenal Disorders.

Using Rome IV criteria, patients with one or more of bothersome symptoms: postprandial fullness, early satiation, epigastric pain and/or burning with no structural disease (including on endoscopy) are diagnosed as having FD.

For a child/adolescent, Rome IV removed the dictum "no evidence for organic disease" in all definitions and replaced it with "after appropriate medical evaluation, the symptoms cannot be attributed to another medical condition".

Rome IV also continues subdividing FD into postprandial distress syndrome (PDS)—characterized by postprandial fullness and early satiation—and epigastric pain syndrome (EPS)—characterized by epigastric pain or burning.

Justification for these two subgroups includes the fact that PDS but not EPS improves with acotiamide (an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) and pathophysiological studies suggesting that PDS is characterized by a higher prevalence of impaired gastric accommodation and raised duodenal eosinophil counts compared with EPS.

In addition, one Chinese study demonstrated different risk factors among the two subgroups based on the Rome III criteria. While those with either PDS and EPS shared risk factors compared to health controls including younger age (OR 0.95; 99.5% CI, 0.93-0.98), use of NSAIDs (OR 6.60; 99.5% CI, 3.13-13.90), anxiety (OR 3.41; 99.5% CI, 2.01-5.77) and concomitant IBS (OR 6.89; 99.5% CI, 3.41-13.94), those with PDS also had a higher risk of HP (OR 1.86; 99.5% CI, 1.01-3.45), unmarried status (OR 4.22; 99.5% CI, 2.02-8.81), sleep disturbance (OR 2.56; 99.5% CI, 1.29-5.07) and depression (OR 2.34; 99.5% CI, 1.04-5.36).
There should be no evidence of structural disease

Patients typically present with "heartburn" or "indigestion" associated with a constellation of symptoms that include upper abdominal pain or discomfort associated with early satiety, nausea, or bloating. Reports of chronic GI bleeding, unintentional weight loss, epigastric mass, difficulty swallowing, persistent vomiting, or anemia warrant immediate referral for EGD and further evaluation. Alarm symptoms, while more prevalent among patients with GI malignancy, do not have high diagnostic accuracy.

History should include quality, duration, and severity of symptoms, associated symptoms and a complete list of current prescribed and nonprescription medications, particularly noting use of NSAIDs. The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) recommends a review for possible medications associated with dyspepsia including calcium antagonists, nitrates, theophylline, bisphosphonates, and corticosteroids as well as NSAIDs

Physical examination is not helpful. Tenderness to light palpation is fairly specific but has low sensitivity. Tenderness to deep palpation is fairly sensitive for non-ulcer dyspepsia but shows low specificity. Overall, clinical diagnosis by a generalist or specialist is not very accurate either.
Distinguish non-ulcer dyspepsia symptoms in the upper GI tract from other significant sources of epigastric discomfort or pain such as angina pectoris.
Patients with predominantly epigastric or retrosternal burning, acid reflux, or "heartburn" symptoms should be treated for GERD.

In one study of 612 patients with functional GI disorder, those with severe bloating were more likely to be female, younger, and have co-existing functional dyspepsia than those with minimal bloating (p <0.05)

Diagnostic testing is used to rule out other causes of dyspepsia such as ulcer or malignancy. Endoscopy is recommended as the initial test for patients age 60 years and older and any patient at increased risk for malignancy. Consider initial EGD for patients with alarm symptoms.

The 2017 American College of Gastroenterology (ACG)/Canadian Association of Gastroenterology (CAG) guidelines on dyspepsia recommend non-invasive HP testing for patients <60 years of age and treatment if positive. The HP stool antigen test is the noninvasive diagnostic test of choice due to lower cost and wider availability compared with the gold standard 13C urea breath test. If the patient is taking a proton pump inhibitor, discontinue it for 2 weeks prior to testing.

GastroPanel®, a blood test measuring pepsinogen I and II, gastrin-17 and HP antibodies, was useful in identifying patients with atrophic gastritis or HP infection among patients with dyspepsia. The test should not be used to determine the severity of atrophic gastritis. Interestingly, GERD appears to be inversely associated with endoscopic gastric atrophy.

Consider immediate EGD for patients 60 years or older and those with alarm symptoms (chronic GI bleeding, unintentional weight loss, lymphadenopathy, difficulty swallowing, persistent vomiting, iron-deficiency anemia, anorexia, history of PUD, family history of GI cancer, or epigastric mass). Discontinue NSAIDS, if using and possible.

Test and treat for HP if <60 years of age. If no alarm features, treat with nonprescription antacids, H2-blockers, or proton-pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy, the latter is preferred as initial therapy by ACG/CAG. If symptoms persist and not already tested, test for HP and treat accordingly.

Authors of a systematic review of management strategies for uninvestigated dyspepsia found 15 eligible RCTs with 6162 adult participants. Although the "test and treat" strategy ranked first, with a relative risk of remaining symptomatic of 0.89; 95% CI, 0.78-1.02, followed by prompt endoscopy, no strategy was significantly less effective. However, participants assigned to "test and treat" were significantly less likely to receive endoscopy than observed with all other strategies except symptom-based management.

Patients younger than 60 years with non-ulcer dyspepsia and no alarm symptoms do not need extensive workup. However, the age threshold can be decreased in men compared to women to avoid missing malignancy.

In a study of 4664 consecutive patients who underwent a first-time upper endoscopy for dyspepsia, alarm features such as persistent vomiting, dysphagia, and GI bleeding/anaemia were strong predictors for malignancy in patients aged <50 years.

Patients under age 60 years who do not present with any alarm symptoms may be treated empirically with antacid or antisecretory therapy for 1 to 2 weeks to evaluate response. Patients over age 60 years with a negative endoscopy should be managed similarly. B

The 2017 ACG/CAG guidelines recommend a trial of a PPI as first-line therapy. If ineffective, tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) or prokinetic therapies can be tried. B Low-quality studies support herbal treatments, Chinese medicines, acupuncture and hypnotherapy. B
Eradicate H. pylori in patients with dyspepsia who are HP positive. A

Consider advising patients who need long-term management of dyspepsia symptoms to use the effective lowest medication dose, try 'as-needed' use, and attempt a return to antacid self-treatment, if appropriate. C
Patients under age 60 years with nonulcer dyspepsia symptoms but no alarm symptoms can be treated with antacids, PPIs, or H2-receptor antagonists.

The 2017 ACG/CAG guidelines recommend a trial of a PPI as first-line therapy. Authors of a Cochrane review of 25 trials found PPIs are more effective than placebo for reduction in symptoms with a NNT of 11, based on moderate-quality evidence.

The symptoms heartburn and acid regurgitation appear to be effectively controlled with PPI and H2-receptor antagonists whereas symptoms of dyspepsia/indigestion, pharyngo-upper esophageal discomfort and fullness while eating may not be controlled.

Patients with dyspepsia who are HP positive, should be treated to eradicate HP infection.In one large RCT, for every 8 patients treated with eradication therapy instead of placebo, one additional patient will have a 50% improvement in symptoms one year later (NNT = 8; 95% CI, 4.6-38.8).

HP-positive dyspepsia : For HP eradication, triple therapy with omeprazole 20 g, clarithromycin 500 mg, and either amoxicillin 1 g or metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days is effective. The Maastricht V/Florence Consensus Conference recommends triple therapy (PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin) unless clarithromycin resistance rate is over 15%. In areas with high clarithromycin resistance, either bismuth-containing quadruple treatments (PPI + metronidazole + tetracycline + bismuth) or nonbismuth quadruple therapy [PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin + metronidazole] for 10 to 14 days are recommended as a first-line therapy.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 25 RCTs to assess the benefits of HP eradication therapy, found symptom improvement during long-term follow-up at ≥1 year (RR 1.24; 95% CI, 1.12-1.37) but not during short-term follow-up at <1 year (RR 1.26; 95% CI, 0.83-1.92).

The 2017 ACG guidelines concurs with use of clarithromycin triple therapy for patients with no previous history of macrolide exposure who reside in areas where clarithromycin resistance is known to be low, but suggest quadruple therapy with PPI, clarithromycin, amoxicillin, and metronidazole for others. For those who experience treatment failure with clarithromycin-based treatment, they recommend bismuth quadruple therapy or levofloxacin salvage regimens.

Another first-line treatment regimen (PPI, amoxicillin 1 g twice daily, and clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily for 10 days) used in 540 consecutive cases had a 70% eradication efficacy. Cases of treatment failure can be treated with omeprazole, clarithromycin, and levofloxacin for 10 days.

In a systematic review and meta-analysis, sequential therapy with amoxicillin plus a PPI for 5 days, followed by clarithromycin and metronidazole or tinidazole for 5 days, had a better eradication rate than standard triple therapy (NNT=6; 95% CI, 5-7). In another meta-analysis, the 3 regimens found to be at least 90% effective were 7 to 14 days of a PPI plus amoxicillin plus clarithromycin plus metronidazole/tinidazole, 10 to 14 days of standard triple therapy plus probiotics, and 10 to 14 days of PPI plus levofloxacin plus antibiotic.

For patients who have had at least two previous HP treatment failures (refractory HP), bismuth-containing quadruple therapy with amoxicillin was noninferior to quadruple therapy with tetracycline in eradication rates (88.5% vs. 87.2%) in one RCT. If bismuth-containing therapy fails as a first-line option, rifabutin- or levofloxacin-containing triple therapy with high-dose PPI and amoxicillin can be considered as a second-line option.

HP-negative dyspepsia: Among patients with dyspepsia who are HP and endoscopy negative, about half of those who are overweight or obese and one fifth of those who are normal weight will respond to a PPI.

H2-blockers and PPIs appear to be equally effective in controlling symptoms in patients without HP infection. H2-blocker therapy is less expensive. Low-dose omeprazole (20 mg) is as effective as 40 mg for initial treatment. One study found that the PPI lansoprazole (compared to placebo) was more effective in patients with a higher body mass index (BMI ≥25) vs. lower BMI (53% response rate and 23% response rate, respectively).
In the emergency department setting, the PPI pantoprazole provided no additional benefit over the conventional GI cocktail in the relief of acute, severe dyspeptic pain.
Long-term continuous treatment with PPI or H2-blocker is inappropriate for non-ulcer dyspepsia.

A trial of a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) is considered second-line therapy for patients with non-ulcer dyspepsia by the 2017 ACG/CAG guidelines; TCA's are a good choice for patients with comorbid symptoms of anxiety or depression. Amitriptyline, desipramine, imipramine (50 mg daily), doxepin, and other tricyclic antidepressants have all been studied (NNT = 3).

Low-dose amitriptyline not only improves dyspepsia symptoms, but also shortens the time to fall asleep in patients with epigastric pain syndrome (EPS), compared with pantoprazole, Therefore, amitriptyline is considered a good candidate for EPS treatment.

Based on an expert panel review of available literature, low to modest doses of TCAs were supported by the strongest evidence for reducing painful functional GI symptoms followed by weaker evidence supporting use of serotonin noradrenergic reuptake inhibitors, with continued treatment for 6 to 12 months to prevent relapse. They also recommended adding a second agent (e.g., quetiapine, aripiprazole, buspirone, α2δ ligand agents) when a single medication was unsuccessful or produced side effects at higher dosages.

In a small RCT, there was no difference in response rate between
nortriptyline
or placebo in management of functional dyspepsia; response rates were similar in both groups (53.6% vs. 57.6%, respectively).

One systemic review and meta-analysis evaluated psychotropic drugs for FD and found some effectiveness with antipsychotics and TCAs, with fewer trials for other agents. More data from high quality RCTs are needed.
An RCT of 72 patients showed that a short course of 8 weeks with pregabalin reduced global symptoms.
Prokinetic agents (e.g., domperidone, metoclopramide) can be tried but studies are of low quality and these agents have significant side effects.

Authors of a meta-analysis of promotility agents found that when optimal test methods were used, these agents significantly accelerated gastric emptying and improved UGI symptoms (mean reduction, 0.25 SD; 95% CI, -0.37 to -0.13).

Acotiamide , an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, may improve symptoms of patients with FD, particularly those with PDS, without major adverse effects (7 trials). The efficacy and safety of acotiamide ER 300 mg once daily vs. acotiamide 100 mg immediate release thrice daily, were similar in one RCT. A significant improvement in quality of life (QOL) over a four-week treatment period was also observed in both groups. It is recommended as a first-line agent by the Japanese Society of Gastroenterology.

In one RCT of patients with both gastroesophageal reflux disease and FD who had persistent symptoms despite 8 weeks of PPI therapy, combination acotiamide 300 mg/day plus the PPI rabeprazole 10 mg/day was as effective in reducing symptoms by ≥50% as doubling the dose of the PPI for 4 weeks (40.8% and 46.9%, respectively).
Tegaserod and mosapride, both 5-HT(4) agonists used in the management of IBS, may be helpful for patients with FD.
Rebamipide, a gastric mucosal protective agent, may partially reduce symptoms and improve QOL in individuals with FD.
Buspirone was more effective than placebo in a small 4-week RCT for FD.

NICE recommends consideration of laparoscopic fundoplication for people who have a confirmed diagnosis of acid reflux and adequate symptom control, but who cannot tolerate or do not wish to continue drug therapy (PPI or acid suppression) long term.

Tradit
ional Chinese medicine appears to be more effective than prokinetic agents, although data quality is poor. The herb Banxiaxiexin Tang appears to be more effective than Western medicine in treating FD, with an odds ratio of 2.75 (95% CI, 1.86-4.07).The Chinese formula Si-Ni-San, which consists of 4 herbs, was shown to be effective for FD based on pooled data (N 2989; OR 3.94; 95% CI, 3.17-4.90). Authors of a meta-analysis of 15 RCTS found Jianpi Liqi therapy to be more effective for FD than comparators including domperidone, omeprazole, and lansoprazole with an OR of 0.34; 95% CI, 0.26-0.45. Xiangsha Liujunzi granules were also more effective than placebo in patients with FD.

In a 12-week RCT, L. gasseri OLL2716-containing yogurt was better than placebo yogurt for improving symptoms of FD in H. pylori-uninfected individuals at 12 weeks (elimination rate for major dyspepsia symptoms was 35.3% and 17.3%, respectively).
An RCT of 132 patients with FD showed Curcuma longa Linn can improve dyspeptic symptoms and quality of life equivalent to omeprazole.

A novel duodenal release formulation of caraway oil and L-menthol (COLM-SST) showed symptom relief in 95% and improved quality of life in 91% of the responders based on a patient-reported outcome questionnaire from 600 patients with FD.

Probiotics appear to improve symptoms of FD, although data are conflicting. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 4 RCTs found a RR of 1.13 (95% CI, 0.99-1.28) for FD symptom improvement. However, an RCT of 94 patients assessing the use of spore forming probiotics in FD found that the clinical response was higher in the probiotics group (48%) compared to placebo (20%), with a RR of 1.95 (95% CI 1.07-4.11).

A 4-week twice daily course of a dietary supplement (also called a dietary integrator) containing sodium alginate, sodium bicarbonate, bromelin and essential oils resulted in improved symptoms for patients with either dysmotility-like or reflux-like non-ulcer dyspepsia.
A meta-analysis of 58 RCT on placebo response rate in FD showed pooled response rates for symptom improvement and complete relief of 44.3% and 15.6%, respectively.
For patients who prefer nonmedicinal options, hypnotherapy can be considered as an alternative for nonulcer dyspepsia in patients who do not have reflux symptoms.

Acupuncture was more effective than sham acupuncture on non-acupoints for treating patients with FD in an RCT. Acupuncture resulted in increased response rate and elimination rate of all three cardinal symptoms among patients with PDS, with sustained efficacy over 12 weeks in patients who received thrice-weekly treatment for 4 weeks. A Cochrane review of 7 studies, 4 comparing acupuncture with medication, found similar efficacy but studies were of low quality.

Authors of a meta-analysis of seven RCTs concluded that electroacupuncture (EA) is better than the placebo (sham-EA) in treating FD. The therapeutic effect of EA on FD was equivalent to that of pharmacological medications, but was safer with fewer adverse reactions.

Among 132 patients with HP-negative refractory FD of the PDS subtype, EA plus on-demand gastrocaine was more effective than on-demand gastrocaine alone in achieving adequate symptom relief at 12 weeks, with a NNT of 2.36; 95% CI, 1.74-3.64.
Cognitive behavioral therapy may have some positive effects, but the effect is not long-lasting.
Authors of a systemic review found insufficient evidence of efficacy of psychological therapies in non-ulcer dyspepsia.

In one Chinese RCT of hospitalized patients with FD, an 8-week nursing intervention called “comfort care” (evaluation and treatment of stressors) compared to usual nursing care was effective in reducing dyspeptic symptoms, increasing gastric emptying rate, improving gastric motility, and reducing self-reported measures of depression and anxiety.
Patients with functional GI disorders demonstrate hypersensitivity to lipids which may induce or exacerbate symptoms.

Among digestive-drug-free subjects, inadequate sleep, weight gain in adulthood, NSAID use, meals immediately prior to sleep, and frequent skipping of breakfast showed significant positive association with most upper GI symptoms. These might be target behaviors for intervention.
Patients with uncomplicated non-ulcer dyspepsia should be advised to quit smoking and consider a trial of alcohol avoidance.

NICE recommends that adults avoid known precipitants associated with their dyspepsia when possible, including smoking, alcohol, coffee, chocolate, fatty foods and being overweight. Some patients may also benefit from raising the head of the bed and having a main meal well before bedtime.
Patients on a low FODMAP diet had better symptom response to postprandial distress syndrome compared with traditional dietary advice (P = 0.04)
Medication is not required for all patients with nonulcer dyspepsia. When medication is initiated, short-term or intermittent treatment courses are recommended.
If symptom relief is not achieved after 4 to 12 weeks of treatment, refer for additional testing and possible EGD.

NICE recommends that adults who need long-term management of dyspepsia symptoms, be encouraged to reduce their use of prescribed medication in a stepwise fashion: by using the effective lowest dose, by trying "as-needed" use when appropriate, and by returning to antacid/alginate self-treatment. Tapering PPIs appears to be the most effective way of discontinuing the drug.

Patients who do not improve following empiric treatment, with or without HP eradication, patients over age 60 years, and those who present with increased risk for malignancy should be referred directly for upper endoscopy. Those under age 60 years with alarm symptoms can also be considered for immediate EGD .
Among patients diagnosed with dyspepsia, 30% remain symptomatic after 7 years while 52% evolve to minor symptoms, IBS, or GERD. B

In a Japanese RCT of 1042 patients with symptoms of FD, 9% had organic lesions found on endoscopy and 28% had symptom resolution within 1 week of endoscopy in those without a specific lesion on endoscopy.
For patients who are HP positive, eradication of the infection seems to be effective in secondary prevention of dyspepsia, with a recurrence rate of 1% to 2%. B

Patients should be told that in 70% of all patients with dyspepsia, no disease can be found on testing or examination. This means that there is no serious disease ongoing, although pain may still be present. B
Those with post-infectious FD are more likely to experience weight loss based on a cohort study of 459 patients with FD, OR = 2.27.
A long-term population-based study demonstrated that those with overlapping symptoms of GERS and FD had lower quality-of-life scores and substantial use of health-care resources.
PPIs can be used in pregnancy.
For children with FD and gastroparesis refractory to medical therapy, permanent gastric electrical stimulation can be considered, based on a case series.

In an RCT involving 149 children (≤18 years) diagnosed with functional abdominal pain disorder, there was a significant difference in pain improvement and improved quality of life when treated with amitriptyline for 12 weeks compared to placebo.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 33 trials with 2657 children with functional abdominal pain disorders found cognitive behavioral therapy more likely than no intervention to successfully treat children (N=334 children; 38% vs 15%; NNT=5; 95% CI 4 - 8) and to decrease pain frequency and intensity, based on low-quality evidence. Hypnotherapy also appeared to be modestly effective for successfully treating children (N=91 children; 56% vs 19%; NNT = 3; 2 - 6).

In an open-label cross-over RCT of 30 children and adolescents with pain of 25 mm or greater due to functional abdominal pain or irritable bowel syndrome, those randomized to placebo with additional details about the placebo used less rescue pain medication than those keeping a symptom diary (6.7% vs. 53%).
